## Reproducibility matters

Reproducibility is a basic tenet of science. In order to establish scientific knowledge,
one has to be able to obtain the same results when repeating an experiment or observational
study under a defined set of conditions. Modern science is increasingly
computational, where reproducibility implies the same inputs 
for an analysis or routine yield the same outputs. The routines are computer
programs that form software running on your machine.

::: {.callout-note collapse=true}
## Non-deterministic outputs

When considering probabilistic outcomes, you are really looking for the same
*distribution* of outputs over many runs.
:::

A necessary condition for being able to repeat a computational analysis is being
able to run the software providing it.  Hence computational reproducibility
tends to have two steps: (i), can the software run on accessible computing
hardware, and (ii), given (i), does the analysis have reproducible results,
e.g., matching over successive runs or an established reference value?  For the
most part, we will be concerned with (i), i.e., the problem of being able to
reliably run software on different computers, which is not at all trivial. It
has implications not only for reproducibility but also the accessibility and
usability of software. The second (ii) often follows from the deterministic
nature of an ideal  (bug-free) computer program, but becomes critical to inspect
in certain cases, e.g., performance benchmarking. 

### Barriers to computing
Installing research software can be troublesome, especially when there is little
developer support or documentation. This can be enough to prevent
one research group from using software from, and so reproducing the results
of, another research group. It can also be a barrier for novices looking to
learn and apply domain-specific tools.
Even experienced users can lose
considerable time to troubleshooting when installing software on a new
device or performing an update.

At many institutions, compute and software are managed by a dedicated
infrastructure or Research Software Engineering (RSE) team. For these teams,
being able to repeatedly deploy software quickly and consistently across many systems
is essential for providing software access for researchers. In many cases,
it is the only way researchers are able to perform their research, since 
the computational demands of scientific routines may be well beyond the
capabilities of personal computing devices or require specialist hardware.

Containers address these problems by running software in a portable and *contained*
environment that is agnostic to many of the details of the system it is running
on.

## Diverse computing environments

In the broadest sense, a computing environment is everything a software program interacts with:
the hardware, the operating system, installed software and all related
configuration. In the context of software development, *environment* is typically used to refer
to the software portion comprising other system packages and
installed software the program may communicate with.

Computing environments used for research are incredibly diverse. Some
researchers will run applications on their personal laptops whilst others will have
dedicated workstations with GPUs provided by their institution. Yet others will
connect to a remote high-performance computing (HPC) cluster to perform
analysis. How can a developer prepare their software to function correctly on
such a wide range of endpoints?

In order for a computer program to run it must interact with:

- Hardware devices, e.g., CPUs and GPUs, facilitated by firmware 
- The operating system, which provides *drivers* to interface between the hardware and software
- Existing software and libraries on the system it requires, known as
  *dependencies*

Incompatibilities can occur at any level. For example, a program may need a
newer version of a library than the one installed, or not support a particular operating
system altogether. Containers address the software levels, but they still share
the host's hardware and operating system kernel, a point we return to in
[Container Concepts](concepts.qmd).

::: {.callout-note collapse=true}
## Programs, packages, libraries, executables, dependencies...

These terms are often used loosely, and overlap. In this course:

- A **program** is a set of instructions a computer can execute
- An **executable** is a file the operating system can run directly, typically a
  program
- A **library** is reusable code that other programs call (for example, NumPy in Python)
- A **package** is a way of distributing code defining a library or program
- A **dependency** is anything a program needs in order to run, including
  libraries and other programs
:::

## Containers as a reproducibility tool

A container includes an application together with all its dependencies as a
single unit called an *image* that runs in a sandboxed environment.  Anyone with
a piece of software called a container runtime can create a new instance of the
application and its environment from the image without having to manage 
dependencies separately.

The process of installing becomes a matter of downloading the image, which
addresses the first component (i) of reproducibility described above. The image is
immutable which supports the second component (ii), since the versions of the
application and all its dependencies are fixed and the same between all
instances. In other words, rather than trying to recreate the same environment
for the software on a new machine, you just share the environment directly.

For infrastructure teams, the same image can be deployed on a laptop, a workstation
or a shared server, which makes software easier to provide to many users.

::: {.callout-warning collapse=true}
## On exact reproducibility

Using containers removes major sources of variations in the environment,
but do not guarantee reproducible outputs. For example, the host kernel
and the container runtime itself may have differences between instances.
:::

## Facilitating FAIR research software

The FAIR principles (findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable) were
first introduced for scientific data [1], and have since been adapted for research
software [2]:

- **F:**  Software, and associated metadata, is easy for both humans and machines to find
- **A:** Software and its metadata are retrievable via standard protocols
- **I:** Software interoperates with other software by exchanging data or
  metadata through standardised interfaces (APIs)
- **R:** Software is both usable and reusable (can be modified or incorporated in
  other software)

Throughout this course we will develop best practices around containers in order to 
achieve FAIR software outputs. 

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding

1. How does running a container compare with traditional software installation?
2. Explain what a computing environment is.
3. (Harder) Give one reason a container might produce different outputs on two machines.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse=true}
## Answers
1. Running containerised software requires only a container runtime such as
   Podman and a downloaded container image. A traditional installation first
   requires you to check that all dependencies are present on your system, then
   to follow the software's installation process. This can vary between operating
   systems, and may involve downloading and extracting archived files, changing
   environment variables and running third-party (possibly untrusted)
   installers.
2.  The sum of hardware and software&mdash;and their configuration&mdash;a particular program
    or user interacts with.
3. For example, differences in the host kernel or the container runtime itself.
:::
